evidence_quotes.quote: The Irrigation Division of the Bureau had drilled some 30 domestic wells on the Papago reservation by the early 1930's. It never had funds to drill all needed wells.

It could respect the local leadership and forget about the well. It could attempt to destroy existing leadership and go ahead with drilling. Or it could attempt to win over the people and wait until it had won agreement before starting.
In this case an administrator successfully instituted a technological change in an administered group belonging to a culture other than his own against the opposition of its leaders.
There was the well, pumping good clear water into the tank. All anyone had to do to get a drink was walk a couple of miles to the well and turn a handle.
A preliminary form of the case was used for teaching purposes in the Field Laboratory in 1949, refined in 1950, and re-written for the present purposes.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines community drinking-water access among Papago Indian (Tohono Au'autam) villages/rancherias in the arid Papagueria region, specifically the introduction of government-drilled domestic wells replacing seasonal mud charcos and distant mountain springs.
criterion_notes.c2: PASSES PLAIN WORDING / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 READING. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study examines administrative and local governance factors: how U.S. Indian Bureau and Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) administrators interacted with traditional Papago village governance institutions (the village Spokesman and council of married men) when planning and siting wells, contrasting participatory consultation with unilateral administrative installation over local leadership opposition. However, under the 2026-10-13 A16 scope clarification, Criterion 2 requires a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation in rule application, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). Here, the paper is an applied-anthropology study of generic rural water infrastructure project delivery and cultural acceptance of technological change; once drilled, access to well water was completely open and unmediated by any legal, tariff, or administrative rule ('All anyone had to do to get a drink was walk a couple of miles to the well and turn a handle').
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative applied-anthropology empirical case study based on Cornell University Field Laboratory field investigation and archival Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) / Papago Indian Agency records (Gu Vo District, 1936-1940), alongside historical sources.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports community-level water availability and adoption outcomes: installation of permanent domestic wells (including some 30 Indian Bureau wells, subsequent CCC wells, and a windmill/storage tank at the pseudonymous village of Chuwk in 1936), transition from covert nighttime use to universal village reliance on well water, and non-installation of a well at another rancheria following negotiated relocation.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (Papago Indian rancherias/villages on the Papago Reservation, primarily Chuwk village), exposure (administrative siting/drilling of domestic wells with vs. against village council/Spokesman agreement), outcome (permanent domestic well installation and community adoption/use of well water), and study design (qualitative anthropological case study) are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English in Human Organization (Winter 1952).

study_design: Qualitative anthropological case study (field investigation and archival agency files)
population_and_sample: Papago Indians (Tohono Au'autam) on the Papago Reservation in Arizona (unit of analysis: village/rancheria, focusing on a primary case study of 'Chuwk' village in the Gu Vo District from 1936 to 1940 and a brief comparison rancheria).
exposure: Administrative introduction and siting of government-drilled domestic wells by U.S. Indian Bureau and Civilian Conservation Corps officials (specifically unilateral well drilling overriding opposition from the traditional village Spokesman and council vs. participatory planning/negotiation).
outcome: Availability of permanent village drinking-water supply (well, windmill and storage tank installation) and community adoption/utilization of well water.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type clarification of Criterion 2. Although this 1952 applied-anthropology case study empirically examines community drinking-water access (government well-drilling on the Papago Reservation) and administrative interaction with indigenous village leadership (passing the plain wording of Criterion 2), its focus is infrastructure project delivery, consultation versus paternalistic project siting, and cultural resistance/acceptance of technological change rather than any legal, regulatory, tariff, tenure, or administrative rule-type mechanism governing water access.
